technical_note.summary: Explains forms, score spaces, interpretation boundaries, data status, and privacy handling without making diagnostic, hiring, or deterministic personality claims.
technical_note.title: Technical Note

entries.body: The FermatMind Enneagram Test provides readable and observable hypotheses about personality patterns. It presents a primary candidate, top three candidates, the full nine-type profile, and close-call comparison before returning the reader to real situations. The technical note explains how modules are derived from response signals and interpretation rules, and which content remains theoretical or provisional.
entries.title: Test target

entries.body: The E105 five-point Likert form uses rating responses to form a full nine-type profile and top three candidates. The FC144 two-option forced-choice form records relative preference signals across paired choices. Both forms have the same evidence status but different response tasks and scoring sources; FC144 does not overwrite E105's primary candidate.
entries.title: E105 and FC144 two forms

entries.body: The score for E105 is derived from Likert intensity, and the score for FC144 is derived from relative preference of pairwise choice. They are both projected into the same result shell, but do not default into the same numerical comparison semantics. This is why same model is not equal to same score space.
entries.title: Score space boundary

entries.body: Dominance Gap describes the relative gap between Top1 and Top2 in the same form and the same score space, and is used to help the system choose a conservative tone of clear, close-call or diffuse. E105 is different from the question types and scoring units of FC144. The gap cannot be used as a unified ruler across forms, groups, or time; nor is it a measurement error range, statistical confidence interval, norm ranking, external validity proof, or personality certainty.
entries.title: Dominance Gap

entries.body: The current system will output clear, close_call, diffuse, low_quality and other explanation ranges. They control the tone of the results page, the visibility of modules, and recommended actions, rather than claiming that a certain number has been absolutely proven. clear means that the explanations of the same form this time are more concentrated; close_call means that they need to be read side by side; diffuse means that the tone of a single number needs to be reduced; low_quality means that the answer signal is not enough to support strong explanations.
entries.title: Confidence Band

entries.body: When Top1 and Top2 are close, the system will not pretend to be more certain than the data, but will enter the task of pair analysis and 7-day observation. close-call is a ambiguity management bit, not a judgment modification mechanism.
entries.title: Close-call

entries.body: Diffuse refers to the simultaneous emergence of multiple type clues in the profile shape, and Top1 and adjacent candidates are not enough to support a strong primary type narrative. It is a state of reduced certainty in the scope of interpretation, not failure, ineffectiveness, confusion, or low-quality responses. The system will shift the reading focus from a single number to the Top 3 common themes, three-center distribution, evidence contrary to recent life, and repeatable observation tasks; only if these clues continue to appear in real situations are they suitable to continue to narrow the interpretation.
entries.title: Diffuse

entries.body: When a true quality signal triggers, the system enters the low_quality boundary. The function of low_quality in P0 is to narrow the tone and recommend retesting the same form, rather than labeling users unreliable.
entries.title: Low-quality

entries.body: Test-retest stability is an indicator that will be tracked in subsequent Technical Notes. P0 first discloses the definition and collection plan, and does not commit to specific stability rate figures in advance. Stability evidence needs to distinguish between retests of the same form, cross-form agreement, short-term status fluctuations, and user feedback; when the sample, time interval, and answer quality are insufficient, the page will not interpret a retest difference as a personality change.
entries.title: Retake Stability

entries.body: The agreement between E105 and FC144 is used to evaluate the overlap between the two question types on Top1 or Top3, rather than proving that the scores can be directly compared between the two. P0 first defines indicators and collection directions, and then evaluates whether to disclose specific indicators based on samples. Agreement can only show the degree of agreement between the two question types in the ranking of candidates, and cannot independently prove the external validity, clinical validity or career prediction ability of the Enneagram model.
entries.title: E105 / FC144 Agreement

entries.body: The user's Day7 resonance feedback and user_confirmed_type will be entered into the history as self-observation evidence for research and content calibration, but will not silently overwrite the primary_candidate. User feedback is an observation layer, not a re-judgment by the system; it can prompt which narratives need to be downgraded, add counterexamples, or rewrite expressions, but it cannot directly equate resonance with measurement accuracy.
entries.title: Resonance Feedback

entries.body: This test is used for understanding personality patterns and self-observation, and is not used for clinical diagnosis, recruitment screening, treatment recommendations, hard judgments on health levels, or absolute personality characterization. Wing, arrow, subtype and development stage languages ​​are only reserved as interpretation layers or future modules in the current version, and no hard judgment will be made. Technical Note's evidence levels are by default divided into: launched product rules, operational indicators being collected, planned stability indicators, and an explanation framework that is only a theoretical background; these levels cannot be mixed into the same certainty.
entries.title: method boundaries

entries.body: Public instructions only use aggregated method metrics and do not expose individual answer payloads, private observation text, or feedback records that can identify individual users. The share page does not display observation private content by default, and user_confirmed_type will not be regarded as the final type of the system. User feedback, sample content, and Technical Note indicators should all comply with the principles of minimum necessity, aggregate display, and traceability; if an indicator is still in the planned or collecting state, the page will only explain the definition and collection direction, and will not display forged numbers.
entries.title: Privacy and data

entries.boundary_copy: Adjacent traction is only used as an expressive color cue near the same primary type, and is not equivalent to formal wing determination, nor can it replace the primary type or Top3 interpretation.
entries.interpretation_boundary: The wing hint is only suitable for helping to read "which side of the same primary type may be closer in expression", and is not suitable for diagnosis, ability evaluation, health level judgment, career screening or relationship risk judgment.
entries.user_facing_boundary: If you see traction on the left and right sides of the primary candidate, you can understand it as the possibility of adjacent types of tone, rhythm or focus in the expression; this does not mean that the system has judged you as a certain wing, nor does it mean that you have a certain subtype.

entries.boundary_copy: The arrow direction bit is currently only used as a placeholder for future modules and does not participate in the interpretation of the current results page, nor does the arrow be written as a judgment of pressure, growth or development path.
entries.user_facing_boundary: The current version will not deduce your pressure direction, growth direction or fixed path based on the arrow; if it is displayed in the future, it will only serve as a theoretical background prompt and require verification in real situations.

entries.boundary_copy: The state spectrum bits are only used for self-calibration and are not equivalent to hard judgment on the development stage.
entries.user_facing_boundary: The system will not directly mark you into a fixed state level; currently it only provides three observation frames: stable, daily, and stressed.

entries.boundary_copy: subtype is temporarily disabled to avoid early hard judgment when evidence is insufficient.
entries.user_facing_boundary: The current version does not give instinctual subtype conclusions, nor does it miswrite lifestyle differences as formal subtype determinations.

entries.average_expression: In most ordinary situations, you may naturally scan deviations, responsibilities, and completions, and wish that things were more organized.
entries.blind_spot_copy: If Type 1 doesn’t emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you’re less proactive in using standards, closures, and long-term responsibilities to calibrate your actions when rules are vague, quality drops, or responsibility boundaries are unclear. It's not a judgment that you lack a sense of principle.
entries.core_logic: As a top-three candidate, Type 1 suggests that standards, responsibility, order, and improvement drew your attention in this response. Treat this as a hypothesis to test in real situations, not proof of a fixed personality or level of ability.

deep_dive.conflict_pattern: In a conflict, you may first focus on facts, standards and how to deal with it. It is recommended to use it as a communication observation point, while supplementing the feelings, needs and perspective of the other party to avoid attributing conflicts to fixed personalities.
deep_dive.core_desire: In Enneagram language, Type 1 is often used to describe a pattern that directs attention to standards, responsibility, order, and room for improvement. If this applies to you, it is better understood as a value orientation and situational clue: you may calibrate your actions more often by "how is more appropriate and reliable" rather than by systematically confirming your intrinsic motivation or personality.
deep_dive.core_fear: Stress cues associated with this pattern usually occur when responsibilities are missed, confusion occurs, standards are relaxed, important issues are passed over, or efforts do not produce clear results. The page can only hint at possible sensitive points, but cannot confirm what you are really "fearful of", nor can it fix an inferred fear as a psychological fact.
deep_dive.defense_pattern: When pressure arises, it may be easier for you to regain a sense of control by checking, correcting, shutting down, making demands on yourself, or clarifying boundaries. What is described here is an observable coping tendency; it may contribute to quality control, or it may become overly stressful in low-stakes situations and cannot be considered a established psychological mechanism or diagnostic conclusion.
deep_dive.growth_principle: Choose a non-critical task this week, and write down in advance the minimum acceptable standards, risk points that must be guarded, and details that can be left blank; after delivery, only review the factual impact, and do not upgrade every flaw to a self-evaluation.
deep_dive.misread_by_others: A common misinterpreted assumption is that your reminders are heard as nitpicking, rather than being understood as reducing rework, risk, or unfairness. It only indicates possible communication gaps.
deep_dive.recovery_action: Recovery actions can start with a low-risk observation: first distinguish between critical risks and non-critical deviations, then choose a small thing that can be postponed, and record whether the results are really out of control.
deep_dive.relationship_script: In a relationship, being reliable, remembering details, and fixing problems may be part of your expression. However, relationship explanations need to go back to specific interactions, and types cannot be used to infer needs, motivations, or modes of getting along.
deep_dive.self_misread: You may interpret every correction as “responsibility” without distinguishing between key risks, aesthetic preferences, and low-impact details. During the review, you can ask: What did you actually protect by insisting on this time? Is there evidence that the consequences were serious, or did it mainly alleviate your own uneasiness.
deep_dive.stress_signal: Signs of stress can start with observable behaviors such as repeated checking, faster reactions to small deviations, Difficulty registering completion, and physical tension.
deep_dive.thirty_day_experiment: In the next thirty days, record the events that "you want to correct immediately but choose to observe first", write down the risk level, actual consequences and feedback from others, and use evidence to modify the standard strength.
deep_dive.work_mechanism: At work, it may be easier for you to first check that standards are clear, processes are enforceable, boundaries of responsibility are respected, and deliveries are of acceptable quality. It may help you explain why you value calibration and correction, but it cannot replace evidence of ability, experience, interests, organizational environment, and performance in judging job fit.

early_warning_signs.body: After checking the same thing over and over again, it’s still difficult to stop at the version that is sufficient.
early_warning_signs.title: Repeated review

early_warning_signs.body: Issues that could have been discussed first were quickly brought to the forefront and needed to be corrected immediately.
early_warning_signs.title: Quick triggering with small deviations

early_warning_signs.body: After completion, you mainly see the gaps, and rarely stop to confirm which parts have met the requirements.
early_warning_signs.title: Difficulty registering completion

early_warning_signs.body: You may first notice that your shoulders, neck, jaw, or breathing tighten, as if you are on constant alert; this is just an observation clue, not a health judgment.
early_warning_signs.title: Signs of body tightness become apparent

growth_costs.body: In a scenario where enough is enough, you may still want to keep adding more money, as if relaxing would lead to a loss; this can serve as a reminder to distinguish between critical risks and low-risk matters.
growth_costs.title: Misinterpret relaxation as failure

growth_costs.body: Under pressure, you may enter the language of right and wrong and standard sooner, and be slower to admit that you are tired; this reminds you to also look at resource consumption when reviewing.
growth_costs.title: Turn fatigue into a matter of principle

growth_costs.body: If everything is handled according to a no-regret standard, the room for recovery and trial and error may be compressed; you can first identify which items really require high standards.
growth_costs.title: High standards take up recovery time

growth_costs.body: In a relationship or collaboration, it may be harder for others to feel your kindness if the first thing they hear is your shortcomings; the order in which you express them affects how feedback is received.
growth_costs.title: Correction obscures care

growth_strengths.body: In scenarios where standards affect quality or boundaries, if you can explain the purpose behind it, it will be easier for others to interpret your persistence as protecting the results rather than simply finding fault.
growth_strengths.title: Turn principles into trustworthy

growth_strengths.body: This type of caution may be valuable when the task involves safety, commitment, or long-term trust, and you don't easily give up the bottom line to short-term efficiency; low-risk scenarios still require distinguishing between necessary standards and excessive efforts.
growth_strengths.title: Maintain quality at key points

growth_strengths.body: When you have the authority and resources, you may not only point out problems, but also be willing to make improvements through updates to processes, documents, or mechanisms.
growth_strengths.title: Put improvement into action

growth_strengths.body: When standards are clearly stated to protect shared boundaries, rather than being used to pressure people or prove who is right, it can make collaboration more stable.
growth_strengths.title: Protect cooperation with a sense of justice

recovery_protocol.body: First sort the problems by risk, and only select the deviation that needs to be dealt with most to move to the next step.
recovery_protocol.title: Key and non-key

recovery_protocol.body: Pick a low-consequence item, allow it to settle into an acceptable version, and record the actual results.
recovery_protocol.title: Do low-risk good-enough exercises

recovery_protocol.body: Leave your seat briefly, move around, or pause typing, and then decide whether you need to continue making changes.
recovery_protocol.title: Leave the high-intensity scene first

small_experiments.body: Record the rest of the problems but don't deal with them right away to see if they really get out of control.
small_experiments.title: Only fix one key issue a day

small_experiments.body: The next time you remind someone, say "Should we look at the risks?" instead of direct judgment.
small_experiments.title: Change suggestions to invitations

small_experiments.body: Write down one thing that has achieved the goal every day, and train your attention not only to look at the deviation.
small_experiments.title: Record good enough evidence

state_spectrum_copy.default_expression: In most ordinary situations, you may scan deviations, responsibilities, and completion levels; the specific intensity needs to be observed in conjunction with task risks.
state_spectrum_copy.stable_expression: When you have more capacity, standards, responsibility and order may become resources for clear action; this is just situational observation language and does not rank you.
state_spectrum_copy.strained_expression: Under mounting pressure, corrections and demands on yourself may increase; this is just a review reminder and does not assign a level.

entries.growth_summary: Keep the criteria that protect real risks, then choose one low-stakes task where “good enough” is explicit. Compare the actual outcome with the failure you predicted.
entries.healthy_expression: When you have more capacity, a sense of standards may manifest as clarity, fairness, reliability, and a willingness to improve the system.
entries.hero_summary: The following content is based on the Enneagram theoretical model and is only suitable as a self-observation hypothesis, not a diagnosis or fixed personality conclusion. A Type 1 result suggests that it may be easier for you to understand yourself and your environment through standards, responsibility, and a sense of improvement; please calibrate based on specific situations, stress levels, and feedback from others.
entries.internal_tension: A common tension is: on the one hand, we value getting things done steadily and clearly; on the other hand, we also need to judge which scenarios allow for incompleteness, trial and error, or temporary letting go.

communication_manual.body: Before pointing out the problem, let’s first talk about what this standard is protecting: less rework, fair division of labor, or preventing risks from being passed through. This makes it easier for the other person to hear your concerns instead of just your corrections.
communication_manual.title: First give the purpose behind the standard

communication_manual.body: If you have three things you want to say, first mark which one must be dealt with and which two are just reminders. Communication will be more like a consultation than a one-time review.
communication_manual.title: Separate musts from recommendations

communication_manual.body: When your tone becomes tougher, you can add, "I'm a little anxious because I'm worried that something will go wrong later." This is not to weaken your position, but to let the other party see that you are not just finding fault.
communication_manual.title: Add your feelings

conflict_trigger_points.body: When the agreed time, division of labor or standards are not fulfilled twice in a row, you may first enter into correction. Check the facts, impact and original agreement first to avoid directly escalating a mistake into a character judgment.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Promises repeatedly broken

conflict_trigger_points.body: You may harden faster when boundaries, processes, or acceptance criteria are temporarily changed. Before conflict, ask: Is this an exception, a trial, or will this be the case in the future?
conflict_trigger_points.title: Temporary changes to rules

conflict_trigger_points.body: When the other person says "it's okay" and "almost" but you see the subsequent risks, it's easy to increase the intensity. First explain the risk level, and then distinguish between the parts that must be repaired and those that can be observed.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Issues downplayed

partner_facing_notes.body: When he repeatedly confirms rules, time, or commitments, he may be putting the relationship into a dependable structure; or it may simply be that the current matter is high-risk. Ask him which step he is most worried about first, rather than directly interpreting it as being picky.
partner_facing_notes.title: Put correction back into specific scenarios

partner_facing_notes.body: If he doesn't remind or correct this time, it doesn't mean he doesn't care; he may also choose to retain flexibility first. You can ask specifically: Do you want me to listen to you now, or do you want me to fix this problem together?
partner_facing_notes.title: If you don’t correct it, you may be leaving space.

relationship_strengths.body: In a relationship with clear agreements and clear responsibilities, it may be easier for you to show that you care by being punctual, honoring your obligations, and handling problems cleanly.
relationship_strengths.title: Put reliability into action

relationship_strengths.body: When an issue will affect each other repeatedly, you may be more willing to discuss it instead of just being superficial. Whether it is helpful still depends on the timing of expression, tone and the state of the other party.
relationship_strengths.title: Willing to face conflicts seriously

relationship_strengths.body: You may quickly see which commitments, proportions or responsibilities need to be clearly stated; this can sometimes reduce misunderstandings, and may also require more explanation of feelings.
relationship_strengths.title: Boundary language is clearer

relationship_strengths.body: Arrangements, reminders, and repairs may be one of the ways you express your care; if the other party needs more emotional response, you still have to go back to the specific interaction to check.
relationship_strengths.title: Attention lies in details

relationship_traps.body: You may be protecting quality or fairness, but if it's an issue right from the start, the other person may feel negated at first. First ask the other party if they are willing to listen to feedback, and then explain the impact of your concerns; repair in the relationship also requires the other party to be willing to respond, rather than just relying on you to make the standards clearer.
relationship_traps.title: Concern is heard as criticism

relationship_traps.body: When you are hurt, you may talk about right and wrong, rules or responsibilities first, but the real disappointment will appear later. You can separate principles and feelings and say: "I feel this is inappropriate and makes me a little disappointed."
relationship_traps.title: Principles cover injuries

relationship_traps.body: When you're anxious to make a relationship better, suggestions may come across as makeover projects. First confirm whether this is something that both parties want to adjust, and avoid taking your ideal order as the only answer to the relationship.
relationship_traps.title: Correction becomes transformation

relationship_traps.body: If you keep suppressing your dissatisfaction in the front, you may increase the intensity all at once later. A more stable approach is to give a light reminder when small deviations occur and give the other party room to explain limitations or misunderstandings.
relationship_traps.title: Hardens after long-term patience

repair_language.body: I just seemed to be finding fault. In fact, what I was worried about was how this incident would affect the next steps. Let me explain the impact clearly first.
repair_language.title: Let me talk about the impact first

repair_language.body: Not every detail needs to be changed right away. Let us first distinguish three categories: must be repaired, can be looked at later, and can be accepted.
repair_language.title: We prioritize

repair_language.body: After I finished talking about the standards, I also want to hear about your restrictions and see how to adjust them in the most practical way this time.
repair_language.title: I also listen to your restrictions

entries.relationship_summary: You may show care through reliability, follow-through, and practical repair. Ask whether the other person experiences those actions as support, correction, or both.
entries.seven_day_question: Over the next 7 days, record a time when you wanted to correct something: were you more worried about quality, responsibility, relationships, or a sense of loss of control?
entries.short_title: Calibrates reality through standards and responsibility
entries.strained_expression: When the load is high, there may be more corrections and demands on yourself; this is just a review reminder and does not assign a level or diagnosis.
entries.surface_impression: Others may notice seriousness, clear principles, and a readiness to correct errors. Check whether those behaviors appear mainly when quality or responsibility is at stake, rather than assuming they define you in every setting.
entries.validation_hook: To test this candidate, notice whether vague rules, lowered quality, or unclear responsibility make it unusually hard for you to relax. Also record counterexamples: situations where you accept an adequate result, revise a standard, or let a minor flaw remain.

collaboration_manual.body: By explaining the risks, impacts, and shared goals before asking a question, you reduce the chance that others will interpret your warning as critical.
collaboration_manual.title: First align “Why should we repair?”

collaboration_manual.body: Dividing suggestions into three categories: need to be addressed, observable, and deferred can help prevent all issues from being pushed to the highest intensity.
collaboration_manual.title: Mark the risk level

collaboration_manual.body: In addition to pointing out deviations, it also explains what state is good enough to make the working boundary clearer.
collaboration_manual.title: Give an acceptable version

ideal_environment.body: The clearer your completion standards, risk levels, and rework conditions are, the more you can focus on high-value issues.
ideal_environment.title: Standards can be discussed

ideal_environment.body: When the team discusses issues with evidence rather than turning feedback into emotional evaluations, your sense of standards is more likely to be caught.
ideal_environment.title: Review based on facts

ideal_environment.body: If the environment allows for 80% delivery and iteration, it is easier for you to practice allocating standard intensity by risk.
ideal_environment.title: Allows distinction between critical and non-critical

leadership_pattern.body: When you are in a leading, coordinating or reminding position, your influence may come from clarifying goals, standards, responsibilities and review mechanisms, so that delivery does not rely solely on personal awareness. It is suitable for use in scenarios where quality risks are high and processes are prone to drift; however, this only affects style cues and does not mean that the system determines that you have leadership capabilities or are suitable for management positions.
leadership_pattern.title: Use standards and review to create influence

leadership_pattern.body: If the feedback only consists of pointing out shortcomings, the team may interpret your advancement as fault-finding. A more stable approach is to explain the risks, trade-offs and next-step criteria at the same time, so that correction becomes a joint learning rather than an individual judgment; whether it is effective also depends on team trust, authorization boundaries and specific expression methods.
leadership_pattern.title: Turn correction into common calibration

managed_by_others.body: When others need to collaborate with you, assign tasks, or make requests, it may be easier to keep you engaged by clearly stating boundaries, priorities, acceptance criteria, and where trial and error are allowed. What is described here is a preference for collaboration. It is not a general prescription for management methods, nor does it necessarily mean that you need a high-control environment.
managed_by_others.title: First align authorization, priority and acceptance criteria

managed_by_others.body: If the standards continue to change, but the accountability remains retroactive, you may get tighter or defensive more quickly. A more negotiable approach is to clearly state the reasons for the change, scope of impact, and adjustment of responsibilities simultaneously, so that corrections can be returned to the facts of the task rather than turning into mutual accusations.
managed_by_others.title: Synchronize responsibilities and basis when changing standards

work_friction_points.body: When you are quick to point out omissions, discrepancies, or inconsistencies, collaborators may first hear "being corrected" rather than hearing that you are protecting the quality of your delivery. A more negotiable approach is to first explain the risks, acceptance criteria, or common goals associated with this piece of feedback, and then distinguish between the parts that must be corrected and those that can be observed later; this is just a clue to communication friction, and it does not mean that you are necessarily picky or that others are necessarily resistant to feedback.
work_friction_points.title: The common goal needs to be stated before reminding

work_friction_points.body: If low-risk details are handled with the same intensity, the team may feel that progress is being slowed down, and you may become drawn further into the details. Problems can be divided into categories such as release risks, rework risks, experience preferences and personal aesthetics, so that standards can become a decision-making tool instead of being equally tight in every scenario.
work_friction_points.title: Standard strength needs to be stratified by risk

work_friction_points.body: When you are not confident about the quality of the delivery, you may repeat inspections, finish the work yourself, or fill in the omissions for others. This can reduce risks in the short term, but may blur the boundaries of responsibility in the long term. A more stable way to collaborate is to clearly write down the inspection items, responsible persons, deadlines and acceptable errors to avoid mistakenly turning your sense of responsibility into the team's unspoken default.
work_friction_points.title: Quality inspection responsibilities need to be explicitly assigned

work_friction_points.body: When standards are unclear, people in charge change, or evaluation criteria are vague, it may be harder to tell when enough is enough. Instead of continuing to pursue complete determination, you can ask for a temporary judgment standard: what must be met in this round, what risks should be accepted, and when to review; this can bring the friction from personality attribution back to the task boundary.
work_friction_points.title: Gray area decision-making requires stopping conditions

work_strengths.body: When requirements, acceptance criteria or delivery standards are still vague, it may be easier for you to break them into checklists, process nodes and review questions to help the team reduce rework.
work_strengths.title: Translate standards into executable steps

work_strengths.body: During pre-delivery reviews, pre-launch inspections, or cross-team handovers, you may first notice inconsistencies, omissions, or gaps in responsibilities.
work_strengths.title: See quality risks in advance

work_strengths.body: When key responsibilities are diluted, verbal commitments change repeatedly, or records of decisions are missing, you may prefer to make boundaries clear and make collaboration less accountable afterwards; whether it is accepted by the team also depends on the way of expression and organizational culture.
work_strengths.title: Maintain boundaries of responsibility

work_strengths.body: During review meetings, quality reviews, or process revisions, you may be used to turning problems into corrective actions instead of just complaining; this is more likely to work in a team that allows for concrete improvements.
work_strengths.title: Drive continuous improvement

workplace_trigger_points.body: When the acceptance criteria, priority, or responsibility boundaries of the same task change repeatedly, and the reasons for the changes are not explained simultaneously, it may be more difficult for you to focus steadily on the delivery itself. This refers to alert cues in the work situation and does not mean that you lack the ability to adapt to change.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Environment: Standards drift frequently

workplace_trigger_points.body: If obvious vulnerabilities, compliance risks, or review conclusions have been ignored for a long time, you may want to increase the intensity of the alerts. The task environment that is more suitable for you usually requires separate discussions between "do it quickly" and "protect the bottom line".
workplace_trigger_points.title: Task: Quality risks are quickly eliminated

workplace_trigger_points.body: When you raise a standard or issue, it may be harder for you to continue to be gentle if the other person directly hears it as critical. At this time, it is necessary to separate the facts, impacts and next step criteria, rather than turning the interaction into who is right and who is wrong.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Relationships: Correction is understood to be personal

entries.work_summary: At work, you may notice standards, process gaps, quality risks, and unclear ownership early. This describes where attention may go.

entries.average_expression: In most ordinary situations, you may pay attention to what others lack, whether the relationship is cold or not, and what you can add.
entries.blind_spot_copy: If Type 2 does not become the main clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: observe whether you are less proactive in using support, care, and requests for clarity to maintain connection when others need responses, collaboration needs filling, or the relationship temperature cools. It’s not a judgment that you’re aloof or don’t care about the relationship.
entries.core_logic: As a top-three candidate, Type 2 suggests that connection, response, care, and being needed drew your attention in this response. Use it as a self-observation hypothesis, not a verdict about your value or relationship motives.

deep_dive.conflict_pattern: During a conflict, you may first pay attention to whether the relationship is hurt and whether you are seen. It is recommended to use this as a communication observation point and practice stating your needs clearly instead of letting the other party guess.
deep_dive.core_desire: In Enneagram language, Two is often used to describe a pattern that directs attention toward connection, responsiveness, supportive roles, and relationship temperature. If this applies to you, it is better understood as a relationship attention cue: you may judge the situation more often by "can I help, is the relationship still flowing?" rather than systematically confirming your intrinsic motivation or source of value.
deep_dive.core_fear: Stress cues associated with this pattern usually occur when contributions go unseen, responses become less frequent, intimacy becomes colder, a support role loses its place, or someone needs to speak but has difficulty expressing it directly. The page can only hint at possible sensitive points, but cannot confirm what you are truly "afraid of", nor can it fix relationship needs into your psychological facts.
deep_dive.defense_pattern: When stress arises, it may be easier for you to restore a sense of connection by taking care of, getting closer, filling in, satisfying others first, or lowering your own needs. What is described here is an observable coping tendency; it may promote collaboration or it may make boundaries and true requests unclear and should not be taken as a established psychological mechanism or diagnostic conclusion.
deep_dive.growth_principle: Before helping someone else this week, first confirm the support they really need, your available boundaries, and the response you hope to receive; if there is no response, do not automatically make additional contributions, but instead make a clear request.
deep_dive.misread_by_others: A common misreading assumption is that your proactive support is taken for granted, or that your loss is reduced to emotion. It only hints at possible gaps in interactions, it doesn't explain others' reactions, and it doesn't crystallize your relationship needs.
deep_dive.recovery_action: Restorative action can start with a small boundary expression: state a specific need in a low-risk relationship and observe how the other person responds.
deep_dive.relationship_script: In a relationship, taking the initiative to care, remembering details, and taking care of needs may be one of your ways of expression. However, relationship explanations need to go back to specific interactions, and types cannot be used to infer needs, motivations, or modes of getting along.
deep_dive.self_misread: You may be confusing "I just want to help" with "I also want to be seen and needed." When reviewing, you can ask: whether the support was explicitly requested this time, and whether you are really willing. If there is no response, does the loss come from the fact of the relationship or from unspoken expectations?
deep_dive.stress_signal: Stress signals can start from observable behaviors such as over-promising, difficulty in refusing, accumulation of grievances, and expecting the other party to notice without being told.
deep_dive.thirty_day_experiment: In the next thirty days, record every "I want to help" scene: write down whether you were asked, your true wishes, expectations in return, and how you felt afterwards, and use evidence to distinguish caring from overfilling.
deep_dive.work_mechanism: At work, it may be easier for you to first sense who lacks support, where collaboration breakpoints occur, and whether the experience of users or colleagues is taken care of. It may help you explain why you take the initiative to step into gaps and maintain relationship dynamics, but it cannot replace evidence of ability, experience, interest, organizational environment and performance to judge job suitability.

early_warning_signs.body: Say yes to the other person before you evaluate your time, energy, and scope of responsibilities.
early_warning_signs.title: Promise too quickly

early_warning_signs.body: Repeatedly think about how much you did and whether the other person saw it, rather than directly checking expectations.
early_warning_signs.title: Start calculating the effort

early_warning_signs.body: You would rather the other party discover your needs proactively rather than stating the request into specific sentences.
early_warning_signs.title: Difficult to express needs directly

early_warning_signs.body: After supporting others, I obviously have no energy left, but I still continue to increase my responses.
early_warning_signs.title: Decreased energy after care

growth_costs.body: When the relationship position is unclear or the response is insufficient, you may do more to confirm that you are important; this suggests the need to separate support from self-worth.
growth_costs.title: Use money to exchange position

growth_costs.body: If the true need is not expressed, it may be difficult for others to respond in time; this is not because the need itself is unreasonable, but that the way of expression needs to be more specific.
growth_costs.title: Need to passively wait for others to discover

growth_costs.body: Even if you don't have enough resources, you may interpret rejection as not being good enough; at this time, you need to distinguish between capability boundaries, relationship commitments, and current remaining energy.
growth_costs.title: Rejection brings guilt

growth_costs.body: When there is no response for a long time, enthusiasm may gradually turn into implicit dissatisfaction; this usually indicates that expectations need to be stated earlier.
growth_costs.title: Disappointment accumulates and turns into grievance

growth_strengths.body: In familiar relationships or high-interaction situations, you may be more likely to notice unspoken difficulties that others have; this still requires checking by asking rather than automatically drawing conclusions for the other person.
growth_strengths.title: Sensitively capture needs

growth_strengths.body: When the other person really needs support and you have spare capacity, you may turn your concern into actions, resources or companionship to make the help more concrete.
growth_strengths.title: Make support concrete

growth_strengths.body: When a relationship is tense but there is still room for communication, you may be willing to build bridges first to help prevent misunderstandings from growing further.
growth_strengths.title: Maintain relationship resilience

growth_strengths.body: When the task pace is too fast or the team ignores tolerance, you may remind everyone to see people and things at the same time, but this does not mean that you are responsible for everyone's emotions.
growth_strengths.title: Make the team more humane

recovery_protocol.body: Before responding to someone else, confirm whether this is a voluntary choice, a commitment of responsibility, or a concern about changes in the relationship.
recovery_protocol.title: Ask yourself first if you are willing

recovery_protocol.body: Write your expectations into a responseable request instead of waiting for the other person to guess.
recovery_protocol.title: Make a specific request

recovery_protocol.body: Set clear boundaries for time outside of supporting others, and don’t give up all your time to relationship demands.
recovery_protocol.title: Keep recovery time

small_experiments.body: Give yourself time to decide whether you can really take it.
small_experiments.title: Delay for ten minutes before agreeing

small_experiments.body: Say "I can't do it this time" in low-stakes situations and see if the relationship remains stable.
small_experiments.title: Practice saying no gently once

small_experiments.body: Also ask others to give you specific feedback to help you determine whether the support is effective.
small_experiments.title: Make gratitude concrete

state_spectrum_copy.default_expression: In most ordinary situations, you may pay attention to the relationship temperature, other people's needs, and where you can fill the gap; the specific intensity needs to be observed in combination with boundaries.
state_spectrum_copy.stable_expression: When you have more capacity, connection and support can become a source of warmth and reciprocity.
state_spectrum_copy.strained_expression: Under mounting pressure, excessive effort and implicit expectations may increase; this is just a review reminder and does not assign a level.

entries.growth_summary: Make support negotiable: state what you can offer, what you cannot, and one concrete request of your own.
entries.healthy_expression: When you have more capacity, a sense of connection may appear as warmth, sensitivity, and the ability to support others as well as express oneself.
entries.hero_summary: The following content is based on the Enneagram theoretical model and is only suitable as a self-observation hypothesis, not a diagnosis or fixed personality conclusion. A Type 2 result suggests that you may more often understand yourself around the role of connection, response, and support; please calibrate it with evidence of real interactions rather than treating it as a relational identity label.
entries.internal_tension: A common tension is: on the one hand, you want the relationship to be warm and responsive, but on the other hand, you also need to have a clear position for your own needs.

communication_manual.body: Don't let the other person guess what they need from your efforts. Directly saying "What do I want you to respond to this time?" is easier to catch than continuing to provide additional care.
communication_manual.title: Turn expectations into requests

communication_manual.body: When you offer to help, also make it clear where you can go and when you need to stop. The clearer the boundaries, the less likely support will turn into an afterthought.
communication_manual.title: First explain the support boundaries

communication_manual.body: You can say "I took the initiative to coordinate these two times, but I didn't get a response, so I was a little disappointed." Concrete facts can reduce the feeling of accusation and let the other person know where to respond.
communication_manual.title: Put the loss next to the facts

conflict_trigger_points.body: After you continuously fill in the gaps, coordinate or take care of details, if the other party does not respond, frustration will easily accumulate. Point out the specific incident first rather than waiting for the emotion to turn into a bill.
conflict_trigger_points.title: The dedication is not seen

conflict_trigger_points.body: When you ask for support and are rejected, you may interpret the rejection as meaning that you are not important. First confirm which thing, time, or relationship the other party is rejecting.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Request denied

conflict_trigger_points.body: When your messages get shorter, your meetings less frequent, or your tone softens, you may want to double down on your efforts. Ask about the reasons for the changes before deciding whether you need more support.
conflict_trigger_points.title: Response suddenly decreased

partner_facing_notes.body: When he takes the initiative to fill in, asks how he feels, or remembers details, he may be expressing his approach; or it may be that this time the responsibility really falls on him. When responding, state clearly what you saw and ask him what he can do.
partner_facing_notes.title: Treat support as a negotiable behavior

partner_facing_notes.body: If he refuses, withholds care, or doesn't respond right away, it doesn't automatically mean he doesn't care. A more reliable way to check is to ask: Do you need space, help, or a specific response from me this time?
partner_facing_notes.title: Distance does not necessarily equal a cooling relationship

relationship_strengths.body: When the other person needs support or the interaction becomes cold, you may be more likely to take the initiative to approach, ask, and fill in; this shows a tendency to pay attention, but it does not mean that you must be responsible for maintaining the temperature of the relationship.
relationship_strengths.title: Proactively respond to relationship signals

relationship_strengths.body: You may notice more quickly when responses decrease, tone changes, or distance increases; these clues need to be confirmed by questioning and cannot be directly taken as the other person’s true thoughts.
relationship_strengths.title: Detect interaction changes earlier

relationship_strengths.body: You might express proximity by remembering preferences, arranging small things, or tending to practical needs; this advantage is more stable when reciprocity and boundaries are clear.
relationship_strengths.title: Express care with details

relationship_strengths.body: When there are cracks in the relationship, you may be willing to open the door to communication first; whether the repair is effective still depends on whether both parties are willing to participate, not on you alone to do more.
relationship_strengths.title: Willing to try to repair the connection

relationship_traps.body: You may express closeness with care, but unspoken needs are difficult to respond to accurately. Replace "I've done so much" in advance with "I need you to help me with something this time."
relationship_traps.title: Need to hide and pay

relationship_traps.body: It is natural to want to be actively seen, but if understanding is taken as proof of love or not, the relationship will become difficult to calibrate. Check first to see if the other person knows what you expect, and then judge whether the response is adequate.
relationship_traps.title: Expect the other party to take the initiative to understand

relationship_traps.body: In order to stay connected, you may take on care that exceeds your physical strength, time, or inclination. Clarify the scope before supporting. Reciprocity does not mean reciprocity every time, but it cannot be borne by only one party for a long time.
relationship_traps.title: Boundaries are diluted by intimacy

relationship_traps.body: After suppressing needs for a long time, expressing can easily turn into rehashing old scores. You can start with a recent specific incident and explain how you hope to share the burden in the future, rather than just proving that you have paid a lot.
relationship_traps.title: Grief with a sense of bill

repair_language.body: I didn't make it clear just now. I actually hope you can respond to this specific matter, rather than asking you to guess what I need.
repair_language.title: I express my expectations

repair_language.body: I am willing to help with these few things, but I need to stop for the rest, or we can arrange for someone else to take over.
repair_language.title: Re-clarification of support scope

repair_language.body: I'm a little disappointed, but I don't want to do more in exchange for a response. Let’s just tell each other what we need this time.
repair_language.title: I won’t pay more for now

entries.relationship_summary: You may show care by checking in, helping, and staying responsive. Compare that intention with the other person's feedback and with whether your own limits remain visible.
entries.seven_day_question: Over the next seven days, record a time when you wanted to do a little more: was that out of a genuine desire, fear of losing connection, or not knowing how to ask directly?
entries.short_title: Tracks connection through response and support
entries.strained_expression: Under high load, overextending, resentment, or unspoken expectations may increase. Treat these as observation cues, not a fixed relationship pattern or severity rating.
entries.surface_impression: Others may notice warmth, attentiveness, and a readiness to help. Check whether support is freely chosen or becomes a way to secure closeness or avoid stating your own needs.
entries.validation_hook: Notice what happens when a contribution goes unrecognized, a reply is delayed, or a relationship cools. Also record times when you set a clear boundary, ask directly for help, or stay connected without taking responsibility for the other person.

collaboration_manual.body: Confirming what the other person actually needs before supporting can reduce the burden of taking too much responsibility for others.
collaboration_manual.title: Ask first if you are needed

collaboration_manual.body: If you want the other person to respond or cooperate, it's clearer to say it directly than to wait for a long time.
collaboration_manual.title: Speak out your expectations

collaboration_manual.body: Being clear about what you can and cannot do protects relationships and energy.
collaboration_manual.title: Set support boundaries

ideal_environment.body: If the team can clearly recognize coordination, user care, and relationship maintenance, it will be easier for you to stay committed.
ideal_environment.title: Support labor to be seen

ideal_environment.body: When rejections, scheduling, and resource constraints can be discussed normally, you don't have to overpay to maintain the relationship.
ideal_environment.title: Boundaries can be respected

ideal_environment.body: A clear response can help you determine whether your input is effective more than a generic thank you.
ideal_environment.title: Feedback is specific and timely

leadership_pattern.body: When you are in a leading or coordinating position, influence can come from seeing member status, connecting resources, tending to a collaborative atmosphere, and making asking for help more likely to occur. It can help teams feel less isolated, but it cannot be understood as a natural fit for managing others, nor is it a substitute for goals, authority, and evidence of performance.
leadership_pattern.title: Use support networks to create influence

leadership_pattern.body: If you are used to using fill-in, comfort, or additional support to maintain progress, the team may be smoother in the short term, but in the long term it will be unclear who is really responsible. A more sustainable way to influence is to explain the scope of support, handover conditions and responsibility boundaries so that investment in the relationship does not become a unspoken default.
leadership_pattern.title: Separate care and empowerment

managed_by_others.body: When others give feedback on your input, pointing out what specific support you have provided and what problems you have solved is usually more likely to be accepted than simply saying "Thank you for your hard work." It indicates your preference for feedback, and it does not mean that you can only rely on external recognition to maintain motivation.
managed_by_others.title: Reduce recognition to specific supporting behaviors

managed_by_others.body: If all coordination, reassurance, or temporary care falls to you by default, you may become increasingly exhausted and find it harder to say no. During collaboration, the time, scope and subsequent successors of the replacement can be clarified to avoid turning relationship investment into invisible responsibilities.
managed_by_others.title: Temporary filling requires confirmation of boundaries

work_friction_points.body: When the team assumes that you will coordinate, comfort, fill in, or take care of emotions, invisible labor will easily accumulate. You can make it clear "what I can support, what I cannot take over in the long term, and who needs to take over", so that help can be returned to assignable tasks instead of becoming a default request for investment in your relationship.
work_friction_points.title: Support work needs to be seen and assigned

work_friction_points.body: If there is no response for a long time, it may be more difficult for you to judge whether you have helped the key points, or you may interpret silence as not being needed. A more practical approach is to agree on a feedback method, such as "Did the support solve the problem this time? Do I need to intervene next time?" to avoid relying solely on a sense of recognition to judge the value of cooperation.
work_friction_points.title: Feedback channels need to be specified

work_friction_points.body: When someone else makes a request, you may see the other person's needs first and evaluate your own capacity later. Rejection can be changed into boundary negotiation: explaining the scope of what can be provided, what cannot be undertaken, and alternative paths; this not only retains the relationship temperature, but also reduces the subsequent friction caused by over-commitment.
work_friction_points.title: Rejection can be changed to boundary negotiation

work_friction_points.body: In order to prevent the relationship from becoming tense, you may delay expressing your disagreement until the problem becomes larger before expressing it all at once. During collaboration, you can express reservations in a low-intensity way in advance, such as "I support this direction, but there is a boundary that needs to be made clear first."
work_friction_points.title: Dissent needs to arise in advance

work_strengths.body: When new people take over, cross-department collaboration occurs, or there is a gap in information transmission, you may be more likely to notice who is stuck, who lacks information, and where support is needed.
work_strengths.title: Seeing gaps in collaboration

work_strengths.body: During rush hours, post-conflict or long-term project exhaustion periods, you may take the initiative to add care, confirm feelings and coordinate communication so that cooperation is not just about delivery; you also need to be careful not to take all the maintenance of relationships on yourself.
work_strengths.title: Maintain team temperature

work_strengths.body: In client conversations, team rituals, or one-on-one collaborations, you may be more likely to remember preferences, concerns, and unspoken needs; these clues help inform communication but do not equate to career fit conclusions.
work_strengths.title: Remember people's details

work_strengths.body: When colleagues encounter obstacles, you often not only say "I understand", but also turn it into concrete help, reminders, resource connections or follow-up; when boundaries are clear, this kind of support is less likely to turn into over-burdening.
work_strengths.title: Put support into action

workplace_trigger_points.body: When the team leaves coordination, emotional care, and temporary closing to you by default without confirming time and boundaries, you may gradually be consumed. What is described here is the role load, not that you have to take on the support role.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Environment: Invisible filling becomes the default

workplace_trigger_points.body: If you invest heavily in communicating, connecting resources, or helping others move forward, but these efforts are never factored into planning and feedback, it may be harder to judge how much to continue investing.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Task: Support work is not included in the priority list

workplace_trigger_points.body: When the other party changes from intensive interaction to cold treatment, or only accepts help without explaining the true needs, you may want to take the initiative to get closer to confirm. A safer approach is to ask for specific feedback rather than automatically increasing efforts.
workplace_trigger_points.title: Relationships: Responses suddenly become cold or vague

If this applies to you, it is better understood as an action organizing cue: you may calibrate your choices more often by "how to move forward and how to be seen as effective" rather than systematically identifying the source of your self-worth.

The page can only hint at possible sensitive points, but cannot confirm what you are really "afraid of", nor can it fix value anxiety as your psychological fact.
deep_dive.defense_pattern: When pressure rises, it may be easier for you to speed up execution, adjust your image, highlight results, suppress fatigue, or turn your attention to the next goal. What is described here is an observable coping tendency; it may lead to rapid execution or long-term postponement of feelings and relationship needs, and it cannot be regarded as a established psychological mechanism or diagnostic conclusion.
deep_dive.growth_principle: Choose a goal this week, and in addition to the result indicators, write down a process indicator and a relationship/recovery boundary; when reviewing, also check the degree of completion, cost, and whether it still meets the true priority.
deep_dive.misread_by_others: A common misunderstood assumption is that others only see your efficiency, sense of purpose, or performance management, and ignore that you may also be under evaluation pressure. It only helps you check communication gaps and cannot judge for others whether you only care about results.
deep_dive.recovery_action: The recovery action can start from a non-performance pause: no optimization or display of results for the time being, only recording current needs, resources and next choices.

deep_dive.stress_signal: Signs of stress can start with observable behavioral checks such as an inability to stop, low feedback anxiety, delayed feelings, and viewing rest as ineffective.
deep_dive.thirty_day_experiment: In the next thirty days, record every situation in which you pursue results: write down the source of the goal, evaluation pressure, true intention, and recovery afterwards, and use evidence to distinguish between high performance and overperformance.

It may help you explain why you value efficiency and visible results, but it is not a substitute for ability, experience, interests, organizational context and evidence of performance in judging job fit.

early_warning_signs.body: When there is no response, you quickly check the results again and again, add explanations, or find new supporting materials.
early_warning_signs.title: Repeatedly confirm after low feedback

early_warning_signs.body: When you encounter a stuck point, you want to maintain normal performance rather than explain the obstacle or ask for help.
early_warning_signs.title: Hidden difficulties

early_warning_signs.body: When you schedule recovery time, you quickly interpret it as falling behind, being unproductive, or not being committed enough.
early_warning_signs.title: Feeling guilty about taking a break

growth_costs.body: When the results are not good, you may be more likely to associate the fluctuation of results with your self-worth; when reviewing, you need to look at the goals, resources, and external conditions at the same time.
growth_costs.title: Give value to results

growth_costs.body: After getting busy, you may later find that you are tired or don't want to continue; this prompts you to place a status check next to the progress check.
growth_costs.title: True feelings are delayed

growth_costs.body: In order to maintain a competent image, you may be reluctant to reveal that you are stuck or need help; this will make support come in later.
growth_costs.title: Image maintenance consumes energy

growth_costs.body: In a close relationship, the other person may first need to be heard, not just solved; task efficiency does not necessarily equal relationship responsiveness.
growth_costs.title: Relationships are task-oriented

growth_strengths.body: In a scenario where the goals are clear and the feedback path is clear, it may be easier for you to advance the plan to visible output.
growth_strengths.title: bring ideas to fruition

growth_strengths.body: When faced with new goals and effective feedback, you may adjust your strategy quickly; if the feedback itself is ambiguous, you still need to check the criteria first.
growth_strengths.title: Adapt quickly to changes

growth_strengths.body: When the team needs to refocus, your sense of purpose may help others see the next step, but it doesn't mean everyone needs the same rhythm.
growth_strengths.title: Activate team momentum

growth_strengths.body: When resources are limited, you might remind the team to focus their time and energy on areas of greater impact, while also retaining an examination of process and relationship costs.
growth_strengths.title: Pay attention to input and output

recovery_protocol.body: Arrange a period of downtime without presentation, optimization, or reporting, and write down in advance when you will return to the task.
recovery_protocol.title: Pause performance tasks

recovery_protocol.body: Write down whether you need more recognition, rest, support, or redefining your goals at this moment.
recovery_protocol.title: Naming real needs

recovery_protocol.body: Turn your attention away from what others think and back to whether the matter is consistent with long-term value and current resources.
recovery_protocol.title: Review value rather than ranking

small_experiments.body: After finishing, stop for ten minutes and don't change it immediately to make it more beautiful.
small_experiments.title: Don’t optimize immediately

small_experiments.body: Name an unresolved problem in a trusted relationship and see if it really hurts value.
small_experiments.title: Expose a stuck point

small_experiments.body: Record a period of time each day that is not productive but has value for recovery or reflection.

A Type 3 result suggests that you may more often understand yourself around goals, results, and feedback; calibrate with specific context and long-term evidence rather than treating achievement narratives as the final word on your personality.
